extraction_notes.note: Theorem 11 (Section 4.1, 'modified ROI') and Theorem 12 (Appendix A.1) state the same bound for the same algorithm; kept one node (the fuller Theorem 12) with Theorem 11 in also_stated_at.
Lemma 26 repeats Lemma 9 word for word but sits in the approximate-oracle analysis with its own proof; kept as separate nodes rather than merging under the repeated-statement rule.
The proofs of Theorems 1, 12, 15 and 10 have no proof environment; each is the prose of its 'Proof of / Analysis of' subsection, with the inner lemmas, claims and their proofs nested as setup steps.

Theorem 15 cites Algorithm alg:roi-weak where threshold-ROI (alg:roi-threshold) is meant, and the proof of Lemma 16 cites eq:i-2 instead of eq:i-1-t; the ref edges follow the labels as written, and AP4 -> TP8 was added by hand.
Related-work results (Nemhauser greedy, Sviridenko, Calinescu, etc.), the prose descriptions of Algorithms UP and modified ROI, and the experimental results were not extracted as nodes.
Eq. (9) is called 'the following known inequality' without a name; kept as an external equation (Eq. (20) repeats it and is in also_stated_at).

nodes.name: Submodular maximization under knapsack constraint (SMK)
nodes.statement: In the study of submodular maximization under knapsack/cost constraints (SMK), there is an additional cost function $c$ over the ground set. The cost function is modular, i.e., $c(S) = \sum_{x \in S} c(x)$. Given a monotone submodular function $f$, a cost function $c$, and a budget $B$,  the goal is to find a set $S$ that maximizes $f(S)$ under the constraint that $c(S) \leq B$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximize monotone submodular $f(S)$ subject to modular cost $c(S)\le B$.

nodes.name: Profit
nodes.statement: However, maximizing the revenue may not guarantee maximal {\em profit}, which is the difference between achieved revenue and the cost.
differentia: between achieved revenue and the cost

nodes.name: Regularized unconstrained submodular maximization (RUSM)
nodes.statement: Thus, an alternate way to formulate the profit maximization problem is to maximize the function $h = f-c$. This maximization problem is known as {\em regularized unconstrained submodular maximization}~\cite{bodek2022maximizing}.
nodes.statement_short: Maximize $h=f-c$ with $f$ monotone submodular and $c$ modular, unconstrained.

nodes.name: Regularized Unconstrained Weakly-Submodular Maximization (RUWSM)
nodes.statement:
Specifically, given $f$ be a monotone weakly submodular function and $c$ be a modular cost function. The \textit{Regularized Unconstrained Weakly-Submodular Maximization} ($\textbf{\sc RUWSM}$) problem is defined:
\[ \textbf{\sc RUWSM} :  arg\,max_{S \subseteq V} f(S)-c(S) \]
nodes.statement_short: Maximize $f(S)-c(S)$ over all $S\subseteq V$ for monotone weakly submodular $f$ and modular $c$.

nodes.name: Regularized Unconstrained Approximate-Submodular Maximization (RUASM)
nodes.statement:
In certain scenarios, evaluating the submodular function $f$ might be intractable, and one may only have the ability to query a surrogate function $\Tilde{f}$ that is \textit{approximate} to $f$ \cite{cohen2014sketch}.  In this case, we refer to the maximization of $f-c$ problem as 
\textit{Regularized Unconstrained Approximate-Submodular Maximization} (\textbf{\sc RUASM}).
nodes.statement_short: Maximize $f-c$ when only an approximate surrogate oracle $\Tilde{f}$ of $f$ is available.

nodes.name: Regularized objective is (weakly) submodular
nodes.statement: When $f$ is monotone (weakly) submodular and $c$ is modular, the function $h=f-c$ is (weakly) submodular.

nodes.name: Inapproximability of maximizing non-positive submodular functions
nodes.statement: Indeed, it is known that the problem of maximizing non-positive submodular functions does not admit constant multiplicative factor approximation algorithms~\cite{papadimitriou1988optimization, feige1998threshold,bodek2022maximizing}.
conclusions: the problem of maximizing non-positive submodular functions does not admit constant multiplicative factor approximation algorithms

nodes.name: Unconstrained distorted greedy (UDG) guarantee
nodes.statement: \citet{harshaw2019submodular} presented a {\em randomized} algorithm referred to as \emph{unconstrained distorted greedy} (UDG) to address the RUWSM problem.  Their algorithm produces a set $S$ such that {\em expected value of $f(S)$} $\geq (1-e^{-\gamma})f({\rm OPT}) - c({\rm OPT})$, and the algorithm makes $\mathcal{O}(n)$ oracle calls to function $f$.
conclusions: Their algorithm produces a set $S$ such that {\em expected value of $f(S)$} $\geq (1-e^{-\gamma})f({\rm OPT}) - c({\rm OPT})$, and the algorithm makes $\mathcal{O}(n)$ oracle calls to function $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Randomized UDG achieves $(1-e^{-\gamma})f(OPT)-c(OPT)$ in expectation with $O(n)$ oracle calls.

nodes.name: ROI-Greedy guarantee
nodes.statement:
Subsequently, \citet{jin2021unconstrained} developed a {\em deterministic} algorithm, referred to as ROI greedy, for addressing
the RUSM problem (when $f$ is submodular). The algorithm produces a set $S$ such that 
$h(S) \geq f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT}) - {c({\rm OPT})}\log \frac{f({\rm OPT})}{c({\rm OPT})}$ within $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ oracle calls to $f$.
conclusions:
The algorithm produces a set $S$ such that 
$h(S) \geq f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT}) - {c({\rm OPT})}\log \frac{f({\rm OPT})}{c({\rm OPT})}$ within $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ oracle calls to $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Deterministic ROI greedy achieves $f(OPT)-c(OPT)-c(OPT)\log(f(OPT)/c(OPT))$ with $O(n^2)$ oracle calls.

nodes.name: Fast deterministic algorithm matching ROI guarantee
nodes.statement: In the context of these works, a natural question arises for the RUWSM problem: {\em Can one design a deterministic algorithm that matches the approximation guarantee of the ROI algorithm while achieving a runtime closer to that of the UDG algorithm?}
nodes.statement_short: Is there a deterministic RUWSM algorithm with ROI's guarantee and near-UDG runtime?

nodes.name: Threshold greedy guarantee (Badanidiyuru-Vondrak)
nodes.statement: \citet{badanidiyuru2014fast} proved that the thresholding technique maintains the quality of results, achieving an approximation ratio of $(1-1/e-\epsilon)$ (as opposed to $(1-1/e)$ by the natural greedy algorithm).
conclusions: the thresholding technique maintains the quality of results, achieving an approximation ratio of $(1-1/e-\epsilon)$

nodes.name: Obstacles to adapting threshold algorithms to RUWSM
nodes.statement_short: Threshold methods need monotone submodular objectives, and a density-initialized global threshold gives unbounded runtime.

nodes.name: Monotone set function
nodes.statement: Given a ground set $V$ of size $n$ and a utility function $f:2^V\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{\geq 0}$, $f$ is monotone if for any subsets $S \subseteq T \subseteq V$, $f(T) \geq f(S)$.
differentia: for any subsets $S \subseteq T \subseteq V$, $f(T) \geq f(S)$

nodes.name: Marginal gain
nodes.statement: The {\em marginal gain} of adding an element $x \in V \setminus S$ into $S\subseteq V$ is $f(\{x\}|S) \triangleq f(S\cup \{x\})-f(S)$.

nodes.name: Marginal gain shorthand $f(x|S)$
nodes.statement: We write $f(\{x\}|S) = f(x|S)$ for brevity.

nodes.name: Normalized set function
nodes.statement: In this paper, we consider normalized $f$, i.e., $f(\emptyset)=0$.

nodes.name: Submodularity
also_stated_at: A function $f$ is (weakly) submodular if, for any set $S \subseteq T \subseteq V$ and any element $x \in V \setminus T$, the marginal gain of the function value of adding $x$ to $S$ is at least the marginal gain in the function value of adding $x$ to a larger set $T$.
nodes.label: def:sub

nodes.name: Diminishing marginal gain inequality
nodes.statement: f(S \cup \{x\})-f(S)\geq f(T \cup \{x\})-f(T).
nodes.label: eq:marginal-gain

nodes.name: Diminishing return
nodes.statement: This property is referred to as {\em diminishing return}.

nodes.name: $\gamma$-weak submodularity (submodularity ratio)
nodes.statement:
A set function $f:2^V \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{\geq 0}$ is $\gamma$-weakly submodular if for every set $S \subseteq T \subseteq V$:
        \begin{equation} \sum\nolimits_{u\in T \setminus S} f(u \mid S)  \geq  \gamma \big(f(T)-f(S)\big).
        \end{equation}
        $\gamma \in (0,1]$ is referred to as the submodularity ratio and $f$ is submodular iff $\gamma=1$.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is $\gamma$-weakly submodular if singleton marginal gains sum to at least $\gamma$ times the joint gain; $\gamma=1$ is submodular.
nodes.label: def:weak-sub

nodes.name: Weak submodularity inequality
nodes.statement: \sum\nolimits_{u\in T \setminus S} f(u \mid S)  \geq  \gamma \big(f(T)-f(S)\big).
nodes.label: eq:weak-submodularity

nodes.name: $\delta$-approximate function
nodes.statement:
A set function $\Tilde{f}$ is $\delta$-approximate to the utility function $f$ if for every $S \subseteq V$,
    \[  |f(S) - \Tilde{f}(S) | \leq \delta \]
also_stated_at: We define the $\delta$-approximate function $\Tilde{f}$ that is within $\delta$-error of the actual oracle $f$.
nodes.label: def:approximate

nodes.name: Modular (linear) cost function
nodes.statement: A cost function $c: 2^V \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ is {\em modular} or {\em linear} if the equality of Eq. (\ref{eq:marginal-gain}) holds.

nodes.name: Density
nodes.statement: The {\em density} of an element $e$ adding to set $S$ is defined to be $\frac{f(e|S)}{c(e)}$.

nodes.name: Maximum and minimum element cost
nodes.statement: Define $c_{max} = \max_{e \in V} c(e)$ and $c_{min} = \min_{e \in V} c(e)$.

nodes.name: Value oracle model
nodes.statement: In this paper, our algorithms are designed under the standard value oracle model, which assumes that an oracle is capable of returning the value $f(S)$ when provided with a set $S \subseteq V$.

nodes.name: Approximate oracle access for RUASM
nodes.statement: For RUASM, we assume the algorithm can only access a $\delta$-approximate oracle for $f$.

nodes.name: Unconstrained Profit (UP) algorithm
input: utility function $f$, cost function $c$, submodularity ratio $\gamma$, error threshold $\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Lazy per-element thresholds via a density priority queue: add an element if its fresh density is within $(1-\epsilon)$ of its key, re-evaluate each at most $\log(n/\gamma\epsilon)/\epsilon$ times.
nodes.label: alg:up

nodes.name: Approximation guarantee of UP for RUWSM
nodes.statement:
Given a monotone $\gamma$-submodular function $f:2^{V} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{\geq 0}$ and a modular cost function $c$, an error threshold $\epsilon \in (0,1)$, after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{\epsilon}\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon})$ oracle calls to $f$,  Algorithm \ref{alg:up} outputs $\Tilde{S}$ such that
    \[f(\Tilde{S})-c(\Tilde{S}) \geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})- \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A\]
    where $A = c({\rm OPT}) \log \frac{f({\rm OPT})}{c({\rm OPT})}$.
conclusions:
after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{\epsilon}\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon})$ oracle calls to $f$,  Algorithm \ref{alg:up} outputs $\Tilde{S}$ such that
    \[f(\Tilde{S})-c(\Tilde{S}) \geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})- \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A\]
    where $A = c({\rm OPT}) \log \frac{f({\rm OPT})}{c({\rm OPT})}$.
nodes.statement_short: UP makes $O(\frac{n}{\epsilon}\log\frac{n}{\gamma\epsilon})$ oracle calls and gets $\gamma(1-\epsilon)f(OPT)-c(OPT)-\frac{A}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}$.
nodes.label: th:unconstrained

nodes.name: Number of iterations $\ell$
nodes.statement: Let $\ell$ be the value of $i$ at the termination of Algorithm \ref{alg:up}.
also_stated_at: Let $\ell$ be the value of $i$ at the termination of Algorithm \ref{alg:up}.

nodes.name: Marginal gain lower bound for UP
nodes.statement:
For all $i \in [1,\ell]$ and if $v_i$ is the element added to $S_{i-1}$, then
\[ 
f(v_i|S_{i-1}) \geq \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_i)}{c({\rm OPT})} \big ( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{i-1}) \big ). 
\]
nodes.statement_short: Each added element gains at least $\gamma(1-\epsilon)\frac{c(v_i)}{c(OPT)}$ of the remaining gap $f(OPT)-f(S_{i-1})$.
nodes.label: lem:marginal-gain

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement_short: Compare $v_i$'s density with each OPT element's via the queue order, then sum using weak submodularity.

nodes.name: Density comparison of added element vs OPT elements
nodes.statement: \frac{f(v_i|S_{i-1})}{c(v_i)}\geq {(1-\epsilon)\tau_i} \geq (1-\epsilon) \frac{f(u|S_{i-1})}{c(u)}.
nodes.label: eq:i-2

nodes.name: Lower bound on $f(S_i)$ for UP
assumptions: $v_i$ is the element added to $S_{i-1}$ and $f(S_{i})=f(S_{i-1} \cup \{v_i\})$
nodes.statement_short: $f(S_i)\ge(1-\prod_s(1-\gamma(1-\epsilon)c(v_i)/c(OPT)))f(OPT)$.
nodes.label: lem:f-Si

nodes.name: Product lower bound on $f(S_i)$
nodes.statement: f(S_{i}) \geq \left(   1- \prod_{s=1}^{i} \left(1- \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_i)}{c({\rm OPT})} \right)   \right) f({\rm OPT}).
nodes.label: eq:f-Si

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma 3
nodes.statement:
We prove this lemma by induction. We verify the base case ($i=1$) using Lemma \ref{lem:marginal-gain}; note that
$f(\emptyset) = 0$. Next, for every $i>1$, as an induction hypothesis, assume $\forall j \in [1, i-1]$, Eq. (\ref{eq:f-Si}) holds. We can express $f(S_{j+1})$ in the form of $f(S_{j+1}) = f(S_j)+f(v_{j+1}|S_j)$, and apply Lemma ~\ref{lem:marginal-gain} to $f(v_{j+1}|S_j)$ and the induction hypothesis to $f(S_j)$ to wrap up the proof. \hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $i$: base case from Lemma 2 with $f(\emptyset)=0$, step by writing $f(S_{j+1})=f(S_j)+f(v_{j+1}|S_j)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
Let $S_\ell$ with size $\ell$ be the set at the termination of Algorithm \ref{alg:up}. We divide the proof of Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} into two cases based on the relationship between $A$ and $c(S_\ell)$. 


\textbf{Case 1}: $\gamma (1-\epsilon)c(S_\ell) < A$.
    Consider each element $u \in {\rm OPT} \setminus S_\ell$ that was not included in $S_\ell$; such an element can be categorized into two sets $O_1$ and $O_2$ with corresponding reasons.
    
     \begin{itemize}
         \item \textit{$O_1$ is the set of elements removed at line 7.\ }\\
     The density of these elements is $\leq \gamma$ at some point before the algorithm ends. Therefore, for $u \in O_1$, if $\frac{f(u|S_u)}{c(u)}$ is the density (key) of $u$ the last time it appears in the priority queue, then we have $S_u \subseteq S_\ell$. By the property of diminishing return, we have
        \begin{equation} \frac{f(u|S_\ell)}{c(u)} \leq \frac{f(u|S_u)}{c(u)} \leq \gamma.
        \end{equation}
        \item \textit{$O_2$ is the set of elements for which the line 18 condition was not satisfied.\ }\\
    In other words, these elements have been evaluated at line 13 for $(\log \frac{n}{\gamma\epsilon})/{\epsilon}$ times. Note that for any $u \in O_2$, the initial density of $u$ in the priority queue is $\frac{f(u)}{c(u)}$. Thus, we have: 
        \begin{equation} \frac{f(u|S_\ell)}{c(u)} \leq \frac{f(u|S_u)}{c(u)} \leq (1-\epsilon)^{\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\epsilon}}  \frac{f(u)}{c(u)}.
        \end{equation}
     
    From Eq. (\ref{eq:o2}), we can further derive $\forall u \in O_2$,
    \begin{align} f(u|S_u) &\leq (1-\epsilon)^{\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\epsilon}} f(u) \nonumber\\
        &\leq (1+\epsilon)^{-\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\epsilon}}f(u) \quad \quad \mbox{\it due to $1-\epsilon \leq \frac{1}{1+\epsilon}$} \nonumber\\
        &\leq (1+\epsilon)^{-\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\log 1+\epsilon}}f(u) \quad \quad \mbox{\it due to $\epsilon \leq \log{1+\epsilon}$}\nonumber\\
        &= (1+\epsilon)^{-\log_{1+\epsilon} \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}f(u) ~~=~~\frac{\gamma \epsilon}{n} f(u).
    \end{align}
    \end{itemize}
    
    Therefore, for Case 1, we have
    \begin{align*}
        f({\rm OPT})-f(S_\ell)-c({\rm OPT}) &\leq \frac{1}{\gamma}\!\!\sum_{u \in {\rm OPT} \setminus S_{\ell}}\!\!\!\!\!\! f(u|S_\ell)-c({\rm OPT})\\
        &\leq \frac{1}{\gamma}\left(\sum_{u \in O_1} f(u|S_\ell)+\sum_{u \in O_2} f(u|S_\ell)\right)-c({\rm OPT})\\
        &\leq \frac{1}{\gamma}\left(\sum_{u \in O_1} f(u|S_\ell)+\sum_{u \in O_2} f(u|S_\ell)\right)-\sum_{u \in O_1} c(u) \\
        &=\left(\sum_{u \in O_1} \frac{1}{\gamma} f(u|S_\ell) - c(u)\right)+\frac{1}{\gamma}\sum_{u \in O_2} f(u|S_\ell)\\
        &\leq 0 + \frac{1}{\gamma} \sum_{u \in O_2} \frac{\gamma \epsilon}{n} f(u) \quad \quad \mbox{\tt from  Eq. (\ref{eq:o1}) and (\ref{eq:derive-o2})}\\
        &\leq \epsilon f({\rm OPT}) .
    \end{align*}
    The first inequality is due to monotonicity and weak-submodularity (Def.~\ref{def:weak-sub}) of $f$.  The last inequality holds because $O_2 \subseteq {\rm OPT}$, $|{\rm OPT}| \leq n$ and $f(u) \leq f({\rm OPT})$ for $u \in {\rm OPT} \setminus S_\ell$. Thus, we have  $f({\rm OPT})-f(S_\ell)-c({\rm OPT}) \leq \frac{1}{\gamma} \sum_{u \in O_2} \frac{\gamma \epsilon}{n} f(u) \leq \epsilon f({\rm OPT})$. 
     
     Combining the above inequality with the Case 1 condition ($\gamma (1-\epsilon)c(S_\ell) < A$), we have 
     \begin{align*}
         f(\Tilde{S})-c(\Tilde{S})& \geq f(S_\ell)-c(S_\ell)\geq (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A.
     \end{align*}
    {This concludes the proof of the theorem for Case 1}. \hfill $\Box$


 
    \textbf{Case 2}: $\gamma (1-\epsilon)c(S_\ell) \geq A$. \\
    In this case, there exist $t\in[1, \ell]$ such that:
    \begin{equation}
        c(S_{t-1})< \frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)} A  \leq c(S_t) \end{equation}
    We further divide Case 2 into two sub-cases: (2.1) and (2.2).

\textbf{Case 2.1}: \textit{For some $j\in [1,t-1]$, $f(S_{j}) \geq \gamma (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})$}.\\
Note that Algorithm~\ref{alg:up} outputs $\Tilde{S} = arg\,max_{S_i, i \in [n]} f(S_i)-c(S_i)$.
Therefore, for some $j\in [1,t-1]$
\begin{align*}
h(\Tilde{S}) &\geq f(S_j) - c(S_j)  \geq \gamma (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-\frac{A}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)} \\
& \geq \gamma (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT}) - c({\rm OPT}) - \frac{A}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)} .
\end{align*}

This concludes the proof of the theorem for sub-case 2.1.  \hfill $\Box$

\textbf{Case 2.2}: \textit{For all $j \in [1,t-1]$, $f(S_{j}) < \gamma (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})$}.\\
As illustrated in the proof path, we have already
proved the Lemmas~\ref{lem:marginal-gain} and \ref{lem:f-Si}. We will now prove the necessary properties conditioned on the sub-case 2.2. The following two claims give the properties of the cost of every single element in set $S_t$.

\begin{claim} Under the Case 2.2, the following holds: $\forall~ j \in [1, t-1]:~ c(v_j) \leq c({\rm OPT})$.
\end{claim}
{\sc Proof Sketch:} We prove this claim by contradiction. Assume there exist some $j \in [1, t-1]$ that $c(v_j)>c({\rm OPT})$. Under Case 2.2 condition, $f(S_j) < \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})$ is true. Then if we apply Lemma~\ref{lem:marginal-gain} to $f(v_j|S_{j-1})$ of $f(S_j)= f(S_{j-1}) + f(v_j|S_{j-1})$, we can derive $f(S_j) \geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})$, which is a contradiction. \hfill $\Box$

        
\begin{claim} Under the Case 2.2, if we denote $B_j = A-\gamma(1-\epsilon) c(S_{j})$, then we have  $c(v_t) > B_{t-1}$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
\begin{align*}
    c(v_t) &= c(S_t) - c(S_{t-1}) \ \geq \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A- c(S_{t-1}) \\
    &= \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}\big(A-\gamma (1-\epsilon)c(S_{t-1})\big) \\
       & \geq   A- \gamma (1-\epsilon)c(S_{t-1})\ = \ B_{t-1}.
\end{align*}
The first inequality follows from the case 2 condition Eq.~(\ref{eq:th1-case2}).
\end{proof}

Next, we present Lemma \ref{lem:h-upper-bound} that upper bounds the optimal objective value $f({\rm OPT}) - c({\rm OPT})$. Furthermore, under the condition of Case 2.2, a corollary that upper bounds $f(S_j)$ can be derived from the lemma. As illustrated in the proof roadmap in Figure \ref{fig:roadmap}, the lemma and corollary are necessary for the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:unconstrained-h_St}, which wraps up the proof of Case 2.2 of the theorem.

\begin{lemma} Under the Case 2.2,

the following holds: for all $j\in [1,t-1]$, if $B_j=A-\gamma(1-\epsilon) c(S_{j})$, then
\[ 
   f({\rm OPT}) - c({\rm OPT}) \leq \frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}). 
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We divide this proof into two cases based on the valuations of $B_j$ and $c({\rm OPT})$.

\begin{itemize}
    \item If \textbf{$B_j > c({\rm OPT})$}: The lemma holds immediately.
    \item If \textbf{$B_j \leq c({\rm OPT})$}: We first solve the right hands side of the inequality by splitting it into a part with $f(S_{j})$ and without $f(S_{j})$. Then we can further apply Lemma~\ref{lem:f-Si} to the former.
\end{itemize}
\begin{align*}
    & \displaystyle\frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}) = \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)f(S_{j}) + \frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}f({\rm OPT})\\
    &\geq  \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)\underbrace{\left(   1- \prod_{k=1}^{j}  \left(1- \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_k)}{c({\rm OPT})} \right)   \right) f({\rm OPT})}_{\mbox{\tt follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:f-Si}}} +\displaystyle\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}f({\rm OPT})\\
        &=f({\rm OPT}) - \displaystyle\left(\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)\prod_{k=1}^{j} \left(1- \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_k)}{c({\rm OPT})} \right)\right)f({\rm OPT})\\
        &=\left( 1- \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)\prod_{k=1}^{j} \left(1- \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_k)}{c({\rm OPT})} \right) \right)f({\rm OPT})\\
        &\geq \left( 1- \displaystyle\left(1- \frac{B_j+\gamma(1-\epsilon)\cdot \sum_{k=1}^{j}c(v_k)}{(j+1)\cdot c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT})
\end{align*}

The last inequality holds due to the following known inequality: 
\begin{equation}
1-\prod_{i=1}^n\left(1-\frac{x_i}{y}\right) \geq 1-\left(1-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i}{n y}\right)^n \end{equation}
where $x_i, y \in \mathbb{R}^{+} \mbox{ and } x_i \leq y \mbox{ for } i \in [n]$.

Consider $\forall k\in [1,j], x_k = \gamma(1-\epsilon) c(v_k)$, $x_{k+1} = B_j$ and $y = c({\rm OPT})$. Note that, 
$\forall k\in [1,j], \gamma(1-\epsilon) c(v_k) \leq c({\rm OPT})$, which follows from Claim~\ref{claim:single-cost} and 
$\gamma(1-\epsilon) \leq 1$. Also, $B_j \leq c({\rm OPT})$ follows from the condition for this case. Therefore, the last inequality can be obtained by applying Eq.~(\ref{eq:prodsum}).

Proceeding further by using the definitions of $B_j$ and modular function $c$, the following derivations wrap up the proof.

\begin{align*}
    &\displaystyle\frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}) \\
    
    &\geq \left( 1- \displaystyle\left(1- \frac{A-\gamma(1-\epsilon)c(S_j)+\gamma(1-\epsilon) \sum_{k=1}^{j}c(v_k)}{(j+1)\cdot c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT})\\
    &= \left( 1- \displaystyle\left( 1- \frac{A}{(j+1)\cdot c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT}) \\
        &= \left( 1- \displaystyle\left( 1- \frac{1}{j+1}\cdot \ln \frac{f({\rm OPT})}{c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT}) \\
        &\geq \left(1- e^{-\ln \displaystyle\frac{f({\rm OPT})}{c({\rm OPT})}}\right)f({\rm OPT}) \quad \quad \mbox{\tt as $(1- \frac{c}{t} )^t \leq e^{-c}$ } \\
        &=\left( 1- \displaystyle\frac{c({\rm OPT})}{f({\rm OPT})} \right)f({\rm OPT})\\
        &= f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT}).
\end{align*}
\end{proof}
      
        
\begin{corollary} Under the Case 2.2,

the following holds: 
for all $j \in  [1, t-1],$ if $B_j=A-\gamma(1-\epsilon) c(S_{j})$ then 
\[f({\rm OPT}) -f(S_{j}) \geq \displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}c({\rm OPT}).\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}

Note that, for the case $f(S_{j}) -c(S_{j})
            \geq \gamma (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A$, Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} holds immediately. 
   Hence, we consider the opposite case:
    \begin{align*}
    f(S_{j}) -c(S_{j}) &\leq f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A\\
    
    
    &=f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})- c(S_{j}) - \frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}B_j\\
    &\leq \displaystyle\frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}) - c(S_{j}) - \frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}B_j .
    \end{align*}
  
    The last inequality is due to Lemma~\ref{lem:h-upper-bound}. 
                
                
                Rearranging the above inequality concludes the proof of the corollary.
                
\end{proof}


The following lemma discharges the proof for Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} for the sub-case 2.2. 

\begin{lemma} Under the case 2.2,

the following holds:
    \[
    f(S_t)-c(S_t) \geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT}) - \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A
    \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Consider $v_t$ the element added to $S_{t-1}$.
\begin{align*}
    & f(S_t)-c(S_t) =f(v_t|S_{t-1})+f(S_{t-1})-{c(S_t)}\\
    &\geq \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{c(v_t)}{c({\rm OPT})} \big ( f({\rm OPT}) \!-\! f(S_{t-1}) \big ) +f(S_{t-1})\!-\!c(S_t)\\
    
    
    &= { \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{B_{t-1}+c(v_t)-B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \big ( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \big )}  +f(S_{t-1})- {\left(\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}(A-B_{t-1})+c(v_t)\right)}. 
\end{align*}
The first inequality holds from Lemma \ref{lem:marginal-gain}. The equality follows from the definition of  $B_{t-1} = A-\gamma (1-\epsilon) c(S_{t-1})$.

Proceeding further from the above inequality, 
\[
\begin{array}{rl}
& f(S_t)-c(S_t) \\
                &\geq  {\gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1})\right)}+ f(S_{t-1})  \\
                &\hfill  + {\gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{c(v_t)-B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \right) }\\
                 
                & \hfill- \displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A-\left(c(v_t)-\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}B_{t-1}\right)\\
                 
                &\geq  \gamma(1-\epsilon)  \underbrace{\left[\displaystyle\frac{B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \right) + f(S_{t-1})\right]}_{\mbox{\tt apply Lemma~\ref{lem:h-upper-bound}}}   \\
                 
                &\hfill + \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{c(v_t)-B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \right) \\
                    &\hfill- {\displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A-\big(c(v_t)-B_{t-1}\big)}\\   
                &\geq \gamma(1-\epsilon) (f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})) - \displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A \\
                &\hfill + \underbrace{\left[c(v_t)-B_{t-1}\right]\left( \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1})}{c({\rm OPT})} -1 \right)}_{\mbox{\tt residual value }}. 
\end{array}
\]

Note that, in Claim \ref{claim:cost-St}, we have established $c(v_t)\geq B_{t-1}$. Furthermore, from Corollary \ref{col:lower-opt}, we know
$f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_j) \geq \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}{c({\rm OPT})}$. Therefore, 



the residual value is non-negative. Hence, 
\begin{align*}
   &f(\Tilde{S})-c(\Tilde{S}) \geq f(S_t)-c(S_t)\geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A.
\end{align*}
\end{proof}
This concludes the proof of Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} for case 2.2. We have proved the approximation guarantee of Theorem \ref{th:unconstrained} for every case. The following lemma finishes the proof of Theorem \ref{th:unconstrained} by bounding the worst-case running time of Algorithm \ref{alg:up}. 

\begin{lemma} The time complexity of Algorithm \ref{alg:up} is 
    
    $\mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{\epsilon} \log \frac{n}{\epsilon \gamma})$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
    As per line 18 of Algorithm \ref{alg:up}, each element $e \in V$ can be evaluated for at most $(\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon})/{\epsilon}$ times. Each such consideration involves one oracle call to the function $f$. Therefore, the maximal total number of oracle calls for $n$ elements is $n \cdot (\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon})/{\epsilon} \in \mathcal{O}(\frac{n}{\epsilon} \log \frac{n}{\epsilon \gamma})$. 
\end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on $\gamma(1-\epsilon)c(S_\ell)$ vs $A$. Case 2.2 rests on Lemma 8, which combines the marginal-gain lemmas, cost claims and the upper bound of Lemma 6.

nodes.name: Split on $A$ vs $c(S_\ell)$
nodes.statement: Let $S_\ell$ with size $\ell$ be the set at the termination of Algorithm \ref{alg:up}. We divide the proof of Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} into two cases based on the relationship between $A$ and $c(S_\ell)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the final set $S_\ell$ and split into two cases by comparing $A$ with $c(S_\ell)$.

nodes.name: Case 1
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Case 1}: $\gamma (1-\epsilon)c(S_\ell) < A$.
    Consider each element $u \in {\rm OPT} \setminus S_\ell$ that was not included in $S_\ell$; such an element can be categorized into two sets $O_1$ and $O_2$ with corresponding reasons.
    
     \begin{itemize}
         \item \textit{$O_1$ is the set of elements removed at line 7.\ }\\
     The density of these elements is $\leq \gamma$ at some point before the algorithm ends. Therefore, for $u \in O_1$, if $\frac{f(u|S_u)}{c(u)}$ is the density (key) of $u$ the last time it appears in the priority queue, then we have $S_u \subseteq S_\ell$. By the property of diminishing return, we have
        \begin{equation} \frac{f(u|S_\ell)}{c(u)} \leq \frac{f(u|S_u)}{c(u)} \leq \gamma.
        \end{equation}
        \item \textit{$O_2$ is the set of elements for which the line 18 condition was not satisfied.\ }\\
    In other words, these elements have been evaluated at line 13 for $(\log \frac{n}{\gamma\epsilon})/{\epsilon}$ times. Note that for any $u \in O_2$, the initial density of $u$ in the priority queue is $\frac{f(u)}{c(u)}$. Thus, we have: 
        \begin{equation} \frac{f(u|S_\ell)}{c(u)} \leq \frac{f(u|S_u)}{c(u)} \leq (1-\epsilon)^{\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\epsilon}}  \frac{f(u)}{c(u)}.
        \end{equation}
     
    From Eq. (\ref{eq:o2}), we can further derive $\forall u \in O_2$,
    \begin{align} f(u|S_u) &\leq (1-\epsilon)^{\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\epsilon}} f(u) \nonumber\\
        &\leq (1+\epsilon)^{-\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\epsilon}}f(u) \quad \quad \mbox{\it due to $1-\epsilon \leq \frac{1}{1+\epsilon}$} \nonumber\\
        &\leq (1+\epsilon)^{-\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\log 1+\epsilon}}f(u) \quad \quad \mbox{\it due to $\epsilon \leq \log{1+\epsilon}$}\nonumber\\
        &= (1+\epsilon)^{-\log_{1+\epsilon} \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}f(u) ~~=~~\frac{\gamma \epsilon}{n} f(u).
    \end{align}
    \end{itemize}
    
    Therefore, for Case 1, we have
    \begin{align*}
        f({\rm OPT})-f(S_\ell)-c({\rm OPT}) &\leq \frac{1}{\gamma}\!\!\sum_{u \in {\rm OPT} \setminus S_{\ell}}\!\!\!\!\!\! f(u|S_\ell)-c({\rm OPT})\\
        &\leq \frac{1}{\gamma}\left(\sum_{u \in O_1} f(u|S_\ell)+\sum_{u \in O_2} f(u|S_\ell)\right)-c({\rm OPT})\\
        &\leq \frac{1}{\gamma}\left(\sum_{u \in O_1} f(u|S_\ell)+\sum_{u \in O_2} f(u|S_\ell)\right)-\sum_{u \in O_1} c(u) \\
        &=\left(\sum_{u \in O_1} \frac{1}{\gamma} f(u|S_\ell) - c(u)\right)+\frac{1}{\gamma}\sum_{u \in O_2} f(u|S_\ell)\\
        &\leq 0 + \frac{1}{\gamma} \sum_{u \in O_2} \frac{\gamma \epsilon}{n} f(u) \quad \quad \mbox{\tt from  Eq. (\ref{eq:o1}) and (\ref{eq:derive-o2})}\\
        &\leq \epsilon f({\rm OPT}) .
    \end{align*}
    The first inequality is due to monotonicity and weak-submodularity (Def.~\ref{def:weak-sub}) of $f$.  The last inequality holds because $O_2 \subseteq {\rm OPT}$, $|{\rm OPT}| \leq n$ and $f(u) \leq f({\rm OPT})$ for $u \in {\rm OPT} \setminus S_\ell$. Thus, we have  $f({\rm OPT})-f(S_\ell)-c({\rm OPT}) \leq \frac{1}{\gamma} \sum_{u \in O_2} \frac{\gamma \epsilon}{n} f(u) \leq \epsilon f({\rm OPT})$. 
     
     Combining the above inequality with the Case 1 condition ($\gamma (1-\epsilon)c(S_\ell) < A$), we have 
     \begin{align*}
         f(\Tilde{S})-c(\Tilde{S})& \geq f(S_\ell)-c(S_\ell)\geq (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A.
     \end{align*}
    {This concludes the proof of the theorem for Case 1}. \hfill $\Box$
nodes.statement_short: Case $\gamma(1-\epsilon)c(S_\ell)<A$: bound unchosen OPT elements and conclude.

nodes.statement:
Consider each element $u \in {\rm OPT} \setminus S_\ell$ that was not included in $S_\ell$; such an element can be categorized into two sets $O_1$ and $O_2$ with corresponding reasons.
    
     \begin{itemize}
         \item \textit{$O_1$ is the set of elements removed at line 7.\ }\\
     The density of these elements is $\leq \gamma$ at some point before the algorithm ends. Therefore, for $u \in O_1$, if $\frac{f(u|S_u)}{c(u)}$ is the density (key) of $u$ the last time it appears in the priority queue, then we have $S_u \subseteq S_\ell$. By the property of diminishing return, we have
        \begin{equation} \frac{f(u|S_\ell)}{c(u)} \leq \frac{f(u|S_u)}{c(u)} \leq \gamma.
        \end{equation}
        \item \textit{$O_2$ is the set of elements for which the line 18 condition was not satisfied.\ }\\
    In other words, these elements have been evaluated at line 13 for $(\log \frac{n}{\gamma\epsilon})/{\epsilon}$ times. Note that for any $u \in O_2$, the initial density of $u$ in the priority queue is $\frac{f(u)}{c(u)}$. Thus, we have: 
        \begin{equation} \frac{f(u|S_\ell)}{c(u)} \leq \frac{f(u|S_u)}{c(u)} \leq (1-\epsilon)^{\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\epsilon}}  \frac{f(u)}{c(u)}.
        \end{equation}
     
    From Eq. (\ref{eq:o2}), we can further derive $\forall u \in O_2$,
    \begin{align} f(u|S_u) &\leq (1-\epsilon)^{\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\epsilon}} f(u) \nonumber\\
        &\leq (1+\epsilon)^{-\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\epsilon}}f(u) \quad \quad \mbox{\it due to $1-\epsilon \leq \frac{1}{1+\epsilon}$} \nonumber\\
        &\leq (1+\epsilon)^{-\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\log 1+\epsilon}}f(u) \quad \quad \mbox{\it due to $\epsilon \leq \log{1+\epsilon}$}\nonumber\\
        &= (1+\epsilon)^{-\log_{1+\epsilon} \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}f(u) ~~=~~\frac{\gamma \epsilon}{n} f(u).
    \end{align}
    \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Split the OPT elements not in $S_\ell$ into $O_1$ (pruned) and $O_2$ (evaluation budget exhausted).

nodes.name: Elements in $O_1$
nodes.statement:
\textit{$O_1$ is the set of elements removed at line 7.\ }\\
     The density of these elements is $\leq \gamma$ at some point before the algorithm ends. Therefore, for $u \in O_1$, if $\frac{f(u|S_u)}{c(u)}$ is the density (key) of $u$ the last time it appears in the priority queue, then we have $S_u \subseteq S_\ell$. By the property of diminishing return, we have
        \begin{equation} \frac{f(u|S_\ell)}{c(u)} \leq \frac{f(u|S_u)}{c(u)} \leq \gamma.
        \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: By diminishing returns, elements of $O_1$ have density at most $\gamma$ w.r.t. $S_\ell$.

nodes.name: Elements in $O_2$
nodes.statement:
\textit{$O_2$ is the set of elements for which the line 18 condition was not satisfied.\ }\\
    In other words, these elements have been evaluated at line 13 for $(\log \frac{n}{\gamma\epsilon})/{\epsilon}$ times. Note that for any $u \in O_2$, the initial density of $u$ in the priority queue is $\frac{f(u)}{c(u)}$. Thus, we have: 
        \begin{equation} \frac{f(u|S_\ell)}{c(u)} \leq \frac{f(u|S_u)}{c(u)} \leq (1-\epsilon)^{\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\epsilon}}  \frac{f(u)}{c(u)}.
        \end{equation}
     
    From Eq. (\ref{eq:o2}), we can further derive $\forall u \in O_2$,
    \begin{align} f(u|S_u) &\leq (1-\epsilon)^{\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\epsilon}} f(u) \nonumber\\
        &\leq (1+\epsilon)^{-\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\epsilon}}f(u) \quad \quad \mbox{\it due to $1-\epsilon \leq \frac{1}{1+\epsilon}$} \nonumber\\
        &\leq (1+\epsilon)^{-\frac{\log \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}{\log 1+\epsilon}}f(u) \quad \quad \mbox{\it due to $\epsilon \leq \log{1+\epsilon}$}\nonumber\\
        &= (1+\epsilon)^{-\log_{1+\epsilon} \frac{n}{\gamma \epsilon}}f(u) ~~=~~\frac{\gamma \epsilon}{n} f(u).
    \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Repeated $(1-\epsilon)$ decay bounds the gain of $O_2$ elements by $\frac{\gamma\epsilon}{n}f(u)$.

nodes.name: Bound the gap
nodes.statement:
Therefore, for Case 1, we have
    \begin{align*}
        f({\rm OPT})-f(S_\ell)-c({\rm OPT}) &\leq \frac{1}{\gamma}\!\!\sum_{u \in {\rm OPT} \setminus S_{\ell}}\!\!\!\!\!\! f(u|S_\ell)-c({\rm OPT})\\
        &\leq \frac{1}{\gamma}\left(\sum_{u \in O_1} f(u|S_\ell)+\sum_{u \in O_2} f(u|S_\ell)\right)-c({\rm OPT})\\
        &\leq \frac{1}{\gamma}\left(\sum_{u \in O_1} f(u|S_\ell)+\sum_{u \in O_2} f(u|S_\ell)\right)-\sum_{u \in O_1} c(u) \\
        &=\left(\sum_{u \in O_1} \frac{1}{\gamma} f(u|S_\ell) - c(u)\right)+\frac{1}{\gamma}\sum_{u \in O_2} f(u|S_\ell)\\
        &\leq 0 + \frac{1}{\gamma} \sum_{u \in O_2} \frac{\gamma \epsilon}{n} f(u) \quad \quad \mbox{\tt from  Eq. (\ref{eq:o1}) and (\ref{eq:derive-o2})}\\
        &\leq \epsilon f({\rm OPT}) .
    \end{align*}
    The first inequality is due to monotonicity and weak-submodularity (Def.~\ref{def:weak-sub}) of $f$.  The last inequality holds because $O_2 \subseteq {\rm OPT}$, $|{\rm OPT}| \leq n$ and $f(u) \leq f({\rm OPT})$ for $u \in {\rm OPT} \setminus S_\ell$. Thus, we have  $f({\rm OPT})-f(S_\ell)-c({\rm OPT}) \leq \frac{1}{\gamma} \sum_{u \in O_2} \frac{\gamma \epsilon}{n} f(u) \leq \epsilon f({\rm OPT})$.
nodes.statement_short: Weak submodularity and the $O_1,O_2$ bounds give $f(OPT)-f(S_\ell)-c(OPT)\le\epsilon f(OPT)$.

nodes.name: Conclude Case 1
nodes.statement_short: Combine with the Case 1 condition to obtain the guarantee.

nodes.name: Case 2
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Case 2}: $\gamma (1-\epsilon)c(S_\ell) \geq A$. \\
    In this case, there exist $t\in[1, \ell]$ such that:
    \begin{equation}
        c(S_{t-1})< \frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)} A  \leq c(S_t) \end{equation}
    We further divide Case 2 into two sub-cases: (2.1) and (2.2).

\textbf{Case 2.1}: \textit{For some $j\in [1,t-1]$, $f(S_{j}) \geq \gamma (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})$}.\\
Note that Algorithm~\ref{alg:up} outputs $\Tilde{S} = arg\,max_{S_i, i \in [n]} f(S_i)-c(S_i)$.
Therefore, for some $j\in [1,t-1]$
\begin{align*}
h(\Tilde{S}) &\geq f(S_j) - c(S_j)  \geq \gamma (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-\frac{A}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)} \\
& \geq \gamma (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT}) - c({\rm OPT}) - \frac{A}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)} .
\end{align*}

This concludes the proof of the theorem for sub-case 2.1.  \hfill $\Box$

\textbf{Case 2.2}: \textit{For all $j \in [1,t-1]$, $f(S_{j}) < \gamma (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})$}.\\
As illustrated in the proof path, we have already
proved the Lemmas~\ref{lem:marginal-gain} and \ref{lem:f-Si}. We will now prove the necessary properties conditioned on the sub-case 2.2. The following two claims give the properties of the cost of every single element in set $S_t$.

\begin{claim} Under the Case 2.2, the following holds: $\forall~ j \in [1, t-1]:~ c(v_j) \leq c({\rm OPT})$.
\end{claim}
{\sc Proof Sketch:} We prove this claim by contradiction. Assume there exist some $j \in [1, t-1]$ that $c(v_j)>c({\rm OPT})$. Under Case 2.2 condition, $f(S_j) < \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})$ is true. Then if we apply Lemma~\ref{lem:marginal-gain} to $f(v_j|S_{j-1})$ of $f(S_j)= f(S_{j-1}) + f(v_j|S_{j-1})$, we can derive $f(S_j) \geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})$, which is a contradiction. \hfill $\Box$

        
\begin{claim} Under the Case 2.2, if we denote $B_j = A-\gamma(1-\epsilon) c(S_{j})$, then we have  $c(v_t) > B_{t-1}$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
\begin{align*}
    c(v_t) &= c(S_t) - c(S_{t-1}) \ \geq \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A- c(S_{t-1}) \\
    &= \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}\big(A-\gamma (1-\epsilon)c(S_{t-1})\big) \\
       & \geq   A- \gamma (1-\epsilon)c(S_{t-1})\ = \ B_{t-1}.
\end{align*}
The first inequality follows from the case 2 condition Eq.~(\ref{eq:th1-case2}).
\end{proof}

Next, we present Lemma \ref{lem:h-upper-bound} that upper bounds the optimal objective value $f({\rm OPT}) - c({\rm OPT})$. Furthermore, under the condition of Case 2.2, a corollary that upper bounds $f(S_j)$ can be derived from the lemma. As illustrated in the proof roadmap in Figure \ref{fig:roadmap}, the lemma and corollary are necessary for the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:unconstrained-h_St}, which wraps up the proof of Case 2.2 of the theorem.

\begin{lemma} Under the Case 2.2,

the following holds: for all $j\in [1,t-1]$, if $B_j=A-\gamma(1-\epsilon) c(S_{j})$, then
\[ 
   f({\rm OPT}) - c({\rm OPT}) \leq \frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}). 
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We divide this proof into two cases based on the valuations of $B_j$ and $c({\rm OPT})$.

\begin{itemize}
    \item If \textbf{$B_j > c({\rm OPT})$}: The lemma holds immediately.
    \item If \textbf{$B_j \leq c({\rm OPT})$}: We first solve the right hands side of the inequality by splitting it into a part with $f(S_{j})$ and without $f(S_{j})$. Then we can further apply Lemma~\ref{lem:f-Si} to the former.
\end{itemize}
\begin{align*}
    & \displaystyle\frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}) = \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)f(S_{j}) + \frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}f({\rm OPT})\\
    &\geq  \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)\underbrace{\left(   1- \prod_{k=1}^{j}  \left(1- \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_k)}{c({\rm OPT})} \right)   \right) f({\rm OPT})}_{\mbox{\tt follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:f-Si}}} +\displaystyle\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}f({\rm OPT})\\
        &=f({\rm OPT}) - \displaystyle\left(\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)\prod_{k=1}^{j} \left(1- \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_k)}{c({\rm OPT})} \right)\right)f({\rm OPT})\\
        &=\left( 1- \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)\prod_{k=1}^{j} \left(1- \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_k)}{c({\rm OPT})} \right) \right)f({\rm OPT})\\
        &\geq \left( 1- \displaystyle\left(1- \frac{B_j+\gamma(1-\epsilon)\cdot \sum_{k=1}^{j}c(v_k)}{(j+1)\cdot c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT})
\end{align*}

The last inequality holds due to the following known inequality: 
\begin{equation}
1-\prod_{i=1}^n\left(1-\frac{x_i}{y}\right) \geq 1-\left(1-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i}{n y}\right)^n \end{equation}
where $x_i, y \in \mathbb{R}^{+} \mbox{ and } x_i \leq y \mbox{ for } i \in [n]$.

Consider $\forall k\in [1,j], x_k = \gamma(1-\epsilon) c(v_k)$, $x_{k+1} = B_j$ and $y = c({\rm OPT})$. Note that, 
$\forall k\in [1,j], \gamma(1-\epsilon) c(v_k) \leq c({\rm OPT})$, which follows from Claim~\ref{claim:single-cost} and 
$\gamma(1-\epsilon) \leq 1$. Also, $B_j \leq c({\rm OPT})$ follows from the condition for this case. Therefore, the last inequality can be obtained by applying Eq.~(\ref{eq:prodsum}).

Proceeding further by using the definitions of $B_j$ and modular function $c$, the following derivations wrap up the proof.

\begin{align*}
    &\displaystyle\frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}) \\
    
    &\geq \left( 1- \displaystyle\left(1- \frac{A-\gamma(1-\epsilon)c(S_j)+\gamma(1-\epsilon) \sum_{k=1}^{j}c(v_k)}{(j+1)\cdot c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT})\\
    &= \left( 1- \displaystyle\left( 1- \frac{A}{(j+1)\cdot c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT}) \\
        &= \left( 1- \displaystyle\left( 1- \frac{1}{j+1}\cdot \ln \frac{f({\rm OPT})}{c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT}) \\
        &\geq \left(1- e^{-\ln \displaystyle\frac{f({\rm OPT})}{c({\rm OPT})}}\right)f({\rm OPT}) \quad \quad \mbox{\tt as $(1- \frac{c}{t} )^t \leq e^{-c}$ } \\
        &=\left( 1- \displaystyle\frac{c({\rm OPT})}{f({\rm OPT})} \right)f({\rm OPT})\\
        &= f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT}).
\end{align*}
\end{proof}
      
        
\begin{corollary} Under the Case 2.2,

the following holds: 
for all $j \in  [1, t-1],$ if $B_j=A-\gamma(1-\epsilon) c(S_{j})$ then 
\[f({\rm OPT}) -f(S_{j}) \geq \displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}c({\rm OPT}).\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}

Note that, for the case $f(S_{j}) -c(S_{j})
            \geq \gamma (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A$, Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} holds immediately. 
   Hence, we consider the opposite case:
    \begin{align*}
    f(S_{j}) -c(S_{j}) &\leq f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A\\
    
    
    &=f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})- c(S_{j}) - \frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}B_j\\
    &\leq \displaystyle\frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}) - c(S_{j}) - \frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}B_j .
    \end{align*}
  
    The last inequality is due to Lemma~\ref{lem:h-upper-bound}. 
                
                
                Rearranging the above inequality concludes the proof of the corollary.
                
\end{proof}


The following lemma discharges the proof for Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} for the sub-case 2.2. 

\begin{lemma} Under the case 2.2,

the following holds:
    \[
    f(S_t)-c(S_t) \geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT}) - \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A
    \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Consider $v_t$ the element added to $S_{t-1}$.
\begin{align*}
    & f(S_t)-c(S_t) =f(v_t|S_{t-1})+f(S_{t-1})-{c(S_t)}\\
    &\geq \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{c(v_t)}{c({\rm OPT})} \big ( f({\rm OPT}) \!-\! f(S_{t-1}) \big ) +f(S_{t-1})\!-\!c(S_t)\\
    
    
    &= { \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{B_{t-1}+c(v_t)-B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \big ( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \big )}  +f(S_{t-1})- {\left(\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}(A-B_{t-1})+c(v_t)\right)}. 
\end{align*}
The first inequality holds from Lemma \ref{lem:marginal-gain}. The equality follows from the definition of  $B_{t-1} = A-\gamma (1-\epsilon) c(S_{t-1})$.

Proceeding further from the above inequality, 
\[
\begin{array}{rl}
& f(S_t)-c(S_t) \\
                &\geq  {\gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1})\right)}+ f(S_{t-1})  \\
                &\hfill  + {\gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{c(v_t)-B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \right) }\\
                 
                & \hfill- \displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A-\left(c(v_t)-\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}B_{t-1}\right)\\
                 
                &\geq  \gamma(1-\epsilon)  \underbrace{\left[\displaystyle\frac{B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \right) + f(S_{t-1})\right]}_{\mbox{\tt apply Lemma~\ref{lem:h-upper-bound}}}   \\
                 
                &\hfill + \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{c(v_t)-B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \right) \\
                    &\hfill- {\displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A-\big(c(v_t)-B_{t-1}\big)}\\   
                &\geq \gamma(1-\epsilon) (f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})) - \displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A \\
                &\hfill + \underbrace{\left[c(v_t)-B_{t-1}\right]\left( \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1})}{c({\rm OPT})} -1 \right)}_{\mbox{\tt residual value }}. 
\end{array}
\]

Note that, in Claim \ref{claim:cost-St}, we have established $c(v_t)\geq B_{t-1}$. Furthermore, from Corollary \ref{col:lower-opt}, we know
$f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_j) \geq \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}{c({\rm OPT})}$. Therefore, 



the residual value is non-negative. Hence, 
\begin{align*}
   &f(\Tilde{S})-c(\Tilde{S}) \geq f(S_t)-c(S_t)\geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A.
\end{align*}
\end{proof}
This concludes the proof of Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} for case 2.2.

        &=f({\rm OPT}) - \displaystyle\left(\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)\prod_{k=1}^{j} \left(1- \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_k)}{c({\rm OPT})} \right)\right)f({\rm OPT})\\
        &=\left( 1- \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)\prod_{k=1}^{j} \left(1- \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_k)}{c({\rm OPT})} \right) \right)f({\rm OPT})\\
        &\geq \left( 1- \displaystyle\left(1- \frac{B_j+\gamma(1-\epsilon)\cdot \sum_{k=1}^{j}c(v_k)}{(j+1)\cdot c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT})
\end{align*}

\begin{equation}
1-\prod_{i=1}^n\left(1-\frac{x_i}{y}\right) \geq 1-\left(1-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i}{n y}\right)^n \end{equation}

Consider $\forall k\in [1,j], x_k = \gamma(1-\epsilon) c(v_k)$, $x_{k+1} = B_j$ and $y = c({\rm OPT})$. Note that,

\begin{align*}
    &\displaystyle\frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}) \\
    
    &\geq \left( 1- \displaystyle\left(1- \frac{A-\gamma(1-\epsilon)c(S_j)+\gamma(1-\epsilon) \sum_{k=1}^{j}c(v_k)}{(j+1)\cdot c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT})\\

\begin{corollary} Under the Case 2.2,

the following holds: 
for all $j \in  [1, t-1],$ if $B_j=A-\gamma(1-\epsilon) c(S_{j})$ then 
\[f({\rm OPT}) -f(S_{j}) \geq \displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}c({\rm OPT}).\]

Note that, for the case $f(S_{j}) -c(S_{j})
            \geq \gamma (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A$, Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} holds immediately. 
   Hence, we consider the opposite case:
    \begin{align*}
    f(S_{j}) -c(S_{j}) &\leq f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A\\
    
    
    &=f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})- c(S_{j}) - \frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}B_j\\
    &\leq \displaystyle\frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}) - c(S_{j}) - \frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}B_j .

    The last inequality is due to Lemma~\ref{lem:h-upper-bound}.

\end{proof}


The following lemma discharges the proof for Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} for the sub-case 2.2. 

\begin{lemma} Under the case 2.2,

the following holds:
    \[
    f(S_t)-c(S_t) \geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT}) - \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A
    \]

    & f(S_t)-c(S_t) =f(v_t|S_{t-1})+f(S_{t-1})-{c(S_t)}\\

    &= { \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{B_{t-1}+c(v_t)-B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \big ( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \big )}  +f(S_{t-1})- {\left(\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}(A-B_{t-1})+c(v_t)\right)}.

Proceeding further from the above inequality, 
\[
\begin{array}{rl}
& f(S_t)-c(S_t) \\
                &\geq  {\gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1})\right)}+ f(S_{t-1})  \\
                &\hfill  + {\gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{c(v_t)-B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \right) }\\
                 
                & \hfill- \displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A-\left(c(v_t)-\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}B_{t-1}\right)\\
                 
                &\geq  \gamma(1-\epsilon)  \underbrace{\left[\displaystyle\frac{B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \right) + f(S_{t-1})\right]}_{\mbox{\tt apply Lemma~\ref{lem:h-upper-bound}}}   \\
                 
                &\hfill + \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{c(v_t)-B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \right) \\
                    &\hfill- {\displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A-\big(c(v_t)-B_{t-1}\big)}\\

\]

Note that, in Claim \ref{claim:cost-St}, we have established $c(v_t)\geq B_{t-1}$. Furthermore, from Corollary \ref{col:lower-opt}, we know
$f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_j) \geq \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}{c({\rm OPT})}$. Therefore, 



the residual value is non-negative. Hence,

   &f(\Tilde{S})-c(\Tilde{S}) \geq f(S_t)-c(S_t)\geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A.

nodes.name: Lemma 6 and Corollary 7
nodes.statement:
Next, we present Lemma \ref{lem:h-upper-bound} that upper bounds the optimal objective value $f({\rm OPT}) - c({\rm OPT})$. Furthermore, under the condition of Case 2.2, a corollary that upper bounds $f(S_j)$ can be derived from the lemma. As illustrated in the proof roadmap in Figure \ref{fig:roadmap}, the lemma and corollary are necessary for the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:unconstrained-h_St}, which wraps up the proof of Case 2.2 of the theorem.

\begin{lemma} Under the Case 2.2,

the following holds: for all $j\in [1,t-1]$, if $B_j=A-\gamma(1-\epsilon) c(S_{j})$, then
\[ 
   f({\rm OPT}) - c({\rm OPT}) \leq \frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}). 
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We divide this proof into two cases based on the valuations of $B_j$ and $c({\rm OPT})$.

\begin{itemize}
    \item If \textbf{$B_j > c({\rm OPT})$}: The lemma holds immediately.
    \item If \textbf{$B_j \leq c({\rm OPT})$}: We first solve the right hands side of the inequality by splitting it into a part with $f(S_{j})$ and without $f(S_{j})$. Then we can further apply Lemma~\ref{lem:f-Si} to the former.
\end{itemize}
\begin{align*}
    & \displaystyle\frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}) = \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)f(S_{j}) + \frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}f({\rm OPT})\\
    &\geq  \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)\underbrace{\left(   1- \prod_{k=1}^{j}  \left(1- \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_k)}{c({\rm OPT})} \right)   \right) f({\rm OPT})}_{\mbox{\tt follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:f-Si}}} +\displaystyle\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}f({\rm OPT})\\
        &=f({\rm OPT}) - \displaystyle\left(\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)\prod_{k=1}^{j} \left(1- \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_k)}{c({\rm OPT})} \right)\right)f({\rm OPT})\\
        &=\left( 1- \displaystyle\left(1-\frac{B_j}{c({\rm OPT})}\right)\prod_{k=1}^{j} \left(1- \gamma(1-\epsilon) \frac{c(v_k)}{c({\rm OPT})} \right) \right)f({\rm OPT})\\
        &\geq \left( 1- \displaystyle\left(1- \frac{B_j+\gamma(1-\epsilon)\cdot \sum_{k=1}^{j}c(v_k)}{(j+1)\cdot c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT})
\end{align*}

The last inequality holds due to the following known inequality: 
\begin{equation}
1-\prod_{i=1}^n\left(1-\frac{x_i}{y}\right) \geq 1-\left(1-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i}{n y}\right)^n \end{equation}
where $x_i, y \in \mathbb{R}^{+} \mbox{ and } x_i \leq y \mbox{ for } i \in [n]$.

Consider $\forall k\in [1,j], x_k = \gamma(1-\epsilon) c(v_k)$, $x_{k+1} = B_j$ and $y = c({\rm OPT})$. Note that, 
$\forall k\in [1,j], \gamma(1-\epsilon) c(v_k) \leq c({\rm OPT})$, which follows from Claim~\ref{claim:single-cost} and 
$\gamma(1-\epsilon) \leq 1$. Also, $B_j \leq c({\rm OPT})$ follows from the condition for this case. Therefore, the last inequality can be obtained by applying Eq.~(\ref{eq:prodsum}).

Proceeding further by using the definitions of $B_j$ and modular function $c$, the following derivations wrap up the proof.

\begin{align*}
    &\displaystyle\frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}) \\
    
    &\geq \left( 1- \displaystyle\left(1- \frac{A-\gamma(1-\epsilon)c(S_j)+\gamma(1-\epsilon) \sum_{k=1}^{j}c(v_k)}{(j+1)\cdot c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT})\\
    &= \left( 1- \displaystyle\left( 1- \frac{A}{(j+1)\cdot c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT}) \\
        &= \left( 1- \displaystyle\left( 1- \frac{1}{j+1}\cdot \ln \frac{f({\rm OPT})}{c({\rm OPT})} \right)^{j+1} \right)f({\rm OPT}) \\
        &\geq \left(1- e^{-\ln \displaystyle\frac{f({\rm OPT})}{c({\rm OPT})}}\right)f({\rm OPT}) \quad \quad \mbox{\tt as $(1- \frac{c}{t} )^t \leq e^{-c}$ } \\
        &=\left( 1- \displaystyle\frac{c({\rm OPT})}{f({\rm OPT})} \right)f({\rm OPT})\\
        &= f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT}).
\end{align*}
\end{proof}
      
        
\begin{corollary} Under the Case 2.2,

the following holds: 
for all $j \in  [1, t-1],$ if $B_j=A-\gamma(1-\epsilon) c(S_{j})$ then 
\[f({\rm OPT}) -f(S_{j}) \geq \displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}c({\rm OPT}).\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}

Note that, for the case $f(S_{j}) -c(S_{j})
            \geq \gamma (1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A$, Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} holds immediately. 
   Hence, we consider the opposite case:
    \begin{align*}
    f(S_{j}) -c(S_{j}) &\leq f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A\\
    
    
    &=f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})- c(S_{j}) - \frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}B_j\\
    &\leq \displaystyle\frac{B_j(f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{j}))}{c({\rm OPT})} +f(S_{j}) - c(S_{j}) - \frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}B_j .
    \end{align*}
  
    The last inequality is due to Lemma~\ref{lem:h-upper-bound}. 
                
                
                Rearranging the above inequality concludes the proof of the corollary.
                
\end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: State and prove Lemma 6 and Corollary 7.

nodes.name: Lemma 8 closes Case 2.2
nodes.statement:
The following lemma discharges the proof for Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} for the sub-case 2.2. 

\begin{lemma} Under the case 2.2,

the following holds:
    \[
    f(S_t)-c(S_t) \geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT}) - \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A
    \]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Consider $v_t$ the element added to $S_{t-1}$.
\begin{align*}
    & f(S_t)-c(S_t) =f(v_t|S_{t-1})+f(S_{t-1})-{c(S_t)}\\
    &\geq \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{c(v_t)}{c({\rm OPT})} \big ( f({\rm OPT}) \!-\! f(S_{t-1}) \big ) +f(S_{t-1})\!-\!c(S_t)\\
    
    
    &= { \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{B_{t-1}+c(v_t)-B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \big ( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \big )}  +f(S_{t-1})- {\left(\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}(A-B_{t-1})+c(v_t)\right)}. 
\end{align*}
The first inequality holds from Lemma \ref{lem:marginal-gain}. The equality follows from the definition of  $B_{t-1} = A-\gamma (1-\epsilon) c(S_{t-1})$.

Proceeding further from the above inequality, 
\[
\begin{array}{rl}
& f(S_t)-c(S_t) \\
                &\geq  {\gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1})\right)}+ f(S_{t-1})  \\
                &\hfill  + {\gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{c(v_t)-B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \right) }\\
                 
                & \hfill- \displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A-\left(c(v_t)-\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}B_{t-1}\right)\\
                 
                &\geq  \gamma(1-\epsilon)  \underbrace{\left[\displaystyle\frac{B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \right) + f(S_{t-1})\right]}_{\mbox{\tt apply Lemma~\ref{lem:h-upper-bound}}}   \\
                 
                &\hfill + \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{c(v_t)-B_{t-1}}{c({\rm OPT})} \left( f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1}) \right) \\
                    &\hfill- {\displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A-\big(c(v_t)-B_{t-1}\big)}\\   
                &\geq \gamma(1-\epsilon) (f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})) - \displaystyle\frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}A \\
                &\hfill + \underbrace{\left[c(v_t)-B_{t-1}\right]\left( \gamma(1-\epsilon) \displaystyle\frac{f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_{t-1})}{c({\rm OPT})} -1 \right)}_{\mbox{\tt residual value }}. 
\end{array}
\]

Note that, in Claim \ref{claim:cost-St}, we have established $c(v_t)\geq B_{t-1}$. Furthermore, from Corollary \ref{col:lower-opt}, we know
$f({\rm OPT}) - f(S_j) \geq \frac{1}{\gamma(1-\epsilon)}{c({\rm OPT})}$. Therefore, 



the residual value is non-negative. Hence, 
\begin{align*}
   &f(\Tilde{S})-c(\Tilde{S}) \geq f(S_t)-c(S_t)\geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})-c({\rm OPT})-\frac{1}{\gamma (1-\epsilon)}A.
\end{align*}
\end{proof}
This concludes the proof of Theorem~\ref{th:unconstrained} for case 2.2.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Claim 4
nodes.statement: We prove this claim by contradiction. Assume there exist some $j \in [1, t-1]$ that $c(v_j)>c({\rm OPT})$. Under Case 2.2 condition, $f(S_j) < \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})$ is true. Then if we apply Lemma~\ref{lem:marginal-gain} to $f(v_j|S_{j-1})$ of $f(S_j)= f(S_{j-1}) + f(v_j|S_{j-1})$, we can derive $f(S_j) \geq \gamma(1-\epsilon)f({\rm OPT})$, which is a contradiction. \hfill $\Box$

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 7
nodes.statement:
